Safari first, golf woven through. We started because the trips we wanted to take did not exist: real safari, real golf, and no one to stitch the two together properly.
Two halves of a day, and a lifetime in Africa.

The first golf safari we ran was for ourselves: a round at Karen on the way to the Mara, because the tee time was there and the flight was not until four. The day had two halves, and both were better for the other.

Since then we have played and slept our way across thirteen countries, walked every course we sell and stayed in every camp. We know which guide to ask for at which lodge, which fairways flood in April, and which border posts to avoid on a Friday. That is the whole of the business: knowing, and then arranging.

We remain small on purpose. Hosted departures never carry more than eight golfers. Tailor-made journeys are handled by one named planner from the first call to the last transfer, and by a local host a message away for every hour in between.

Fancourt's flagship reopened with new bunkering and a firmer, faster surface. It plays two shots harder into the wind and is better for it.

We played the Links three times in the fortnight after it reopened, twice into a south-easter and once in the flat calm that George gives you perhaps one morning in ten. The work is subtle from the tee and obvious from the fairway: the bunkers have been rebuilt with revetted faces and deeper floors, the greens are firmer, and the run-offs that used to hold a ball now feed it away.

The practical effect is that the course rewards a running approach again, which is what Gary Player intended and what a decade of soft conditions had quietly taken away. Into the wind, a well-struck seven iron now lands short and releases; the same shot flown to the flag finishes over the back. Our guests with links experience loved it. Our parkland players needed a round to adjust.

Our advice for the journeys: play Montagu first, the Links second, and take the caddie. The caddies have been walking the new run-offs for months and will save you three shots before the turn. Handicap certificates are checked at the desk, so bring the paper or the app.
When to see the Mara crossings
The herds have been arriving earlier each year. Late July into September is now the safest window, with the conservancies quietest in the second half.

The Great Migration does not run to a calendar, but it does run to grass, and the grass has been greening earlier in the northern Serengeti for several seasons. In 2026 the first big crossings on the Mara River were in the second week of July, a fortnight ahead of the long-term average. By mid August the herds were spread across the Mara Triangle and the conservancies to the north.

For a golf safari the timing matters twice. First for the crossings themselves, which are a probability rather than a promise: three or four full days on the river in August gives you a strong chance, one day gives you a coin toss. Second for the courses in Nairobi, which are at their best in the dry July to September window and can be heavy after the short rains in November.

Our Kenya Classic hosted departure for August 2027 is built on this: four nights on the Mara side, with the golf before rather than after so nobody is checking a phone on the 14th tee for news of a crossing.
Chobe by boat, not by road
In the dry season the riverfront is the whole show. We now put every Chobe afternoon on the water and keep the 4x4 for dawn.

Chobe holds the largest elephant population in Africa, and from June to October almost all of it is within a kilometre of the river. The road along the riverfront is a good drive, but it is also the busiest road in Botswana in the afternoon, and a herd crossing to the islands is best seen from the water at their eye level.

Chobe Game Lodge runs a fleet of quiet electric boats, which changes the experience completely. You sit in the reeds while the elephants swim past the bow, and the only sound is the water. Buffalo, hippo, crocodile and the fish eagles are all closer than any vehicle can get.

So the Falls & Fairways journey now has the morning drives inland for lion and sable, and every afternoon on the river, ending with sundowners as the herds come down. Golfers coming from Elephant Hills the day before find it the perfect counterweight.
Packing clubs for Africa: what actually works
Bring your own clubs if you can. Here is how to do it without carrying them onto a twelve-seat aircraft.

Most of our guests want their own clubs for Fancourt or Leopard Creek and could not care less what they play at Skukuza. The answer is a hard travel case for the international flight, and then letting us move the clubs by road or scheduled freight between the golf legs while you fly light aircraft into the bush with a soft bag.

Light aircraft in Kenya, Tanzania and Botswana have a 15 kilogram soft-bag limit and no room for a club case. Rather than argue at the airstrip, we send the clubs ahead to the next course and they are waiting in the pro shop when you land. On the Grand Crossing the clubs make the trip from Fancourt to Leopard Creek to Elephant Hills to Karen without you touching them.

If you would rather not travel with clubs at all, every course we use has quality rental sets, and we can hold one set for you across a whole journey so the feel does not change. Tell us your specification when you enquire and we will confirm what each course can provide.
How we build a golf-safari day so that neither half feels like the price of the other.

The oldest objection to a golf safari is that it must be a compromise: too little golf for the golfer, too little bush for the non-golfer. It is a fair objection to a badly built day, and most of the golf-and-safari packages we see are badly built, with the round bolted onto a rest day and the game drive squeezed into the hour before dinner.

Our day starts in the wild. First light is when the animals move and the temperature is kind, so the morning drive leaves at six and is back by ten. The round begins at eleven, when the light is high and the fairways are empty, and finishes by four. The evening belongs to the bush again: a short drive, sundowners, dinner outside.

Where the course and the camp are not in the same place, we do not split the day. We split the journey: three golf days in a row, then four safari days, with the clubs moved ahead. The non-golfers get the spa, the vineyard or another drive on the golf days, and the group meets for lunch. Everyone comes home full.
Mauritius after the Open: why October is the month
The DP World Tour leaves Heritage in December. Play it in October, when the courses are tournament-ready and the island is dry.

Le Château is prepared for the AfrAsia Bank Mauritius Open from September, so from October the greens are at tournament speed and the rough is up. It is the best month to see the course as the professionals do. It is also the last month before the summer humidity arrives and the afternoon showers become reliable.

La Réserve, opened above Le Château in 2023, plays very differently: shorter, hillier, with more shot-making and more views. We recommend Le Château on the first day and La Réserve on the second, then a rest day before the boat to Ile aux Cerfs.

Combined with Kruger, October is also the end of the dry season and the best game viewing of the year, which is why the Mauritius & Kruger journey and its hosted departure sit in late September and October. The flights via Johannesburg connect the same day.
The 12th, a long par 4 that turns through a stand of indigenous trees to a green sitting beneath the Ngong Hills.

Laid out on part of Karen Blixen's old coffee estate, the course keeps the plantation's mature trees and its sense of distance from the city. At altitude the ball flies ten per cent further, which flatters the drive and punishes the approach.

Kenya's oldest club and the home of the Kenya Open until 2019. Narrow, mature and fiercely protected by its trees; a course that rewards position over power and has humbled better players than most of us.

Carved through indigenous forest on the north side of Nairobi, with colobus monkeys in the canopy and fairways that stay green through the dry season. The hotel beside the first tee makes it the natural last round before an evening flight.

The Baobab Course is the only PGA-accredited layout in East Africa, set on a ridge north of Mombasa with the ocean on the horizon from nearly every hole. Built for the heat, with wide corridors, paspalum turf and a breeze that arrives after lunch.
The 5th, a downhill par 4 with the whole of Lake Naivasha below the green.
The highest course on our list, set on the escarpment above Lake Naivasha. Zebra and giraffe graze the rough, and the thin air adds thirty yards to a well-struck drive. The lodge sits on the 1st tee.
The par-5 18th, played straight at Kilimanjaro with zebra on the fairway and the clubhouse behind the green.

Set on a private wildlife estate between Arusha and the mountain. David Jones routed the holes so that the mountain appears behind five greens; the wildebeest and zebra do as they please. The course opens most of our Tanzania journeys.
The 7th, a short par 4 along the cliff with the reef below and the mangroves on the left.
Nine ocean-side holes on Zanzibar's north-west coast, designed by Peter Matkovich for a resort course that is more fun than it has any right to be. Play it twice before lunch and the beach after.
The par-3 17th, played over a burn to a green ringed by pot bunkers, the hole Ernie Els and Tiger Woods halved in the 2003 Presidents Cup.

Gary Player's answer to the question of whether a links can be built on a flat field: 700,000 cubic metres of earth moved to make dunes, hollows and a routing that changes direction with every hole. Ranked number one in South Africa since it opened, and played walking with a caddie, as it should be.
The par-5 2nd, a double dog-leg with water at the green that sets the tone for the round.

The original Fancourt course, refined by David McLay Kidd into a parkland that sits comfortably among the country's top five. Softer than the Links, with the Outeniqua mountains behind every green and water on half the holes.
The 16th, a short par 4 with the lake on the right and a green that asks for one more club.
The friendliest of Fancourt's three, with wide fairways and water on ten holes. The round to play on arrival day, when the clubs have just come out of the case.
The 18th, a par 4 with the Berg River on the left and the Simonsberg filling the sky behind the green.

A Jack Nicklaus signature course among the Paarl vineyards and the host of three South African Opens. Big, generous and beautifully kept, with the mountains close enough to touch and a wine farm at the clubhouse door.
The par-5 13th along the Crocodile River, where the green sits above a bend in the water and the Kruger elephants cross the far bank.

Gary Player's bushveld masterpiece on the southern boundary of Kruger. A private club that we open by invitation, with hippos below the 13th, crocodiles sunning on the bank and a halfway house that looks into the park. Host of the Alfred Dunhill Championship.
The 9th, a par 4 along the Lake Panic dam with hippos in the water and a sign that reads 'beware of the animals'.

The only unfenced course inside Kruger National Park, built for the park's staff and open to visitors by arrangement. Nine holes played twice, with impala on the fairway and a ranger walking the round. Not a championship test, and one of the most memorable rounds in the world.
The par-5 8th along the Bot River lagoon, with the Kogelberg mountains across the water.

An hour from Cape Town on the Bot River lagoon, with the back nine running along the water and a finish that is among the best in the country. The hotel sits on the course, which makes an early tee time easy.
The 10th, played straight uphill towards the Helderberg with the whole of False Bay at your back.

Gary Player's Winelands course at the foot of the Helderberg, host of the 1996 World Cup of Golf. A front nine on the flat and a back nine that climbs into the mountain, with views of the bay from the top.
The 15th, where the spray of the Falls rises above the trees behind the green.

Ten minutes from Victoria Falls, with warthogs rooting in the rough, impala on the fairways and the Zambezi beside the back nine. The only course in the world where you can see the spray of a natural wonder from the tee.
The par-3 12th over a rock-ringed pond, the postcard hole.
Harare's championship estate course, designed by Peter Matkovich among granite kopjes and msasa woodland. The round for guests routing through the capital on the way to Mana Pools.
The par-5 7th, with the lagoon beyond the green and the whole Bel Ombre estate below.

The home of the AfrAsia Bank Mauritius Open on the DP World Tour, on the Bel Ombre estate in the island's south. The Indian Ocean is visible from every hole; the Black River mountains frame the inland holes. Play it in October when the greens are at tournament speed.
The 16th, a short par 4 played downhill towards the lagoon with the ocean filling the view.
Opened in 2023 in the hills above Le Château, designed by Peter Matkovich with Louis Oosthuizen. Shorter, hillier and more about shot-making than its sibling, with the best views on the island.
The 9th, a par 4 along the lagoon with volcanic rock and the mountains of the east coast across the water.

Bernhard Langer's island course, reached by boat from the Touessrok jetty, with the lagoon in play on nine holes and a volcanic-rock garden where other courses have rough. Lunch at the beach club afterwards is part of the round.
The 6th, a par 3 across the ocean's edge with Ile aux Cerfs on the horizon.

Ernie Els' east-coast course, with six holes along the ocean and the rest among the mangroves and sugar fields. Quieter than its neighbour across the water, and in better condition than almost anything on the island.
The 10th, a par 4 along the lake shore with the marabou storks in the trees.

East Africa's oldest course, on the shore of Lake Victoria a short walk from the hotel. A gentle, mature parkland where the vervet monkeys steal balls and the storks ignore everyone. The round before the flight to Bwindi.
The 5th, a long par 4 across the Kitante stream to a raised green in the middle of the city.

Host of the Uganda Open in the centre of Kampala, with a stream that crosses eight fairways and a hill that makes the back nine feel longer than its card. An optional round for those with a night in the capital.
The par-3 14th over a ravine to a green cut into the hillside.

Rebuilt by Gary Player Design from the old Nyarutarama course into the best-conditioned layout in East Africa, ten minutes from the city centre. Rolling, well bunkered and built for championship play, with the thousand hills as the backdrop.
The 17th, a par 5 with water down the left and the clubhouse behind the green.
Gaborone's championship course, designed by Peter Matkovich on the edge of the city with lakes on eight holes. The round for guests routing through the capital before the Delta.
The 6th, a par 4 where the zebra graze between the tee and the fairway bunkers.
Ten minutes from the Zambian side of the Falls, with zebra and impala on the fairways and a colonial clubhouse that has not changed in decades. The course is simple; the setting is not.

Host of the Zambia Open, a mature parkland course on the way to the Lower Zambezi with jacaranda-lined fairways and fast, true greens. Busy at weekends; we book weekday mornings.

The capital's championship course on the edge of the Khomas highlands, with the thin air of 1,650 metres adding length and the mountains on the skyline. The opening round before the drive to Sossusvlei.
The 8th, a par 4 cut between two dunes with the Namib on both sides and the Atlantic fog rolling in.

One of only a handful of true desert courses in the world: green fairways cut into the Namib dunes beside the Swakop River, with springbok on the practice ground and the sea fog as a morning hazard. Nothing else in Africa plays like it.
The 7th on the old course, a par 4 between cypress and olive with the snow of the Atlas behind the green.

The oldest course in the south, laid out under the Pasha of Marrakech in 1923 and extended to 27 holes. Narrow corridors of cypress, palm, olive and orange trees, with the Atlas on the skyline from the back tees. Churchill and Eisenhower both played here.
The par-3 12th, played across a dry wadi to a green with the whole Atlas range behind it.

Niall Cameron's desert course in the foothills above the Agafay, fifteen minutes from the medina and regularly ranked the best course in Morocco. Firm, fast and natural, with the mountains filling the view from every tee.
The 18th, a par 4 along the water to a green beside the sculpture garden.
Kyle Phillips' course ten minutes from the city, with contemporary sculpture set among the water features and a clubhouse built like a riad. Easy on the body and the eye: the round for arrival day.
The 9th on the Red Course, a par 3 to an island green in a lake full of water lilies.

Robert Trent Jones Sr.'s Red Course in Rabat's cork-oak forest is the country's championship test and the home of the Hassan II Trophy and the Lalla Meryem Cup. Long, tree-lined and immaculate, with 45 holes on the estate in all.
The 15th, a par 4 along the Atlantic with the beach on the left and the wind doing what it likes.
Gary Player's links-style course on the dunes at El Jadida, an hour south of Casablanca, with the ocean on one side and the resort on the other. Wide, firm and windy: a links in all but the turf.
The 11th, a par 3 across a ravine on the cliff edge with the surf of Taghazout below.

Kyle Phillips' clifftop course north of Agadir, with argan trees between the fairways and the Atlantic beneath the greens. The best coastal round in the country and the reason to add Taghazout to a Marrakech trip.

Jack Nicklaus Design's course among the cedar forests of Ifrane in the Middle Atlas, at 1,650 metres. Cool, green and alpine, with snow on the greens in January and the macaques of the national park on the fairway edges.

Safari at its most vast. Kilimanjaro Golf opens the trip, then wildlife on a scale nowhere else can match, finished with a descent into the Ngorongoro Crater. Zanzibar adds nine ocean-side holes and a beach.
Gorillas in the forest, golf on the shore of Lake Victoria.
East Africa's oldest course beside the lake, then the single most affecting hour in travel with a mountain gorilla family in Bwindi. Works on its own or as a three-night addition to Kenya.
The gentlest gorilla trek, and a Player-designed course in the capital.
Volcanoes National Park is two hours from Kigali on good roads, and Kigali Golf Resort is the best-conditioned course in East Africa. Akagera adds a classic savanna safari a short drive east.
A round beside the Zambezi with the spray of the Falls on the horizon.

Elephant Hills is the only course in the world within sight of a natural wonder. Hwange and Mana Pools are among the wildest, least crowded parks in Africa, and the Falls themselves need no introduction.
The Okavango by mokoro, Chobe by boat, elephants by the thousand.

Botswana sells exclusivity: few vehicles, private concessions, and water-based safari that no other country offers. The golf is across the border at Victoria Falls, a ninety-minute transfer from Chobe.
Walking safaris in the Luangwa, and golf on the Zambian side of the Falls.
South Luangwa invented the walking safari and still does it best. Livingstone has a championship course ten minutes from the Falls, and the Lower Zambezi offers canoeing among elephants.
Desert golf, the dunes of Sossusvlei, and Etosha's floodlit waterholes.
The emptiest country on the list. Two courses, one in the capital and one in the dunes at Swakopmund, bracket a self-drive or fly-in safari through landscapes that look like nowhere else on earth.

Host of the DP World Tour, with more championship golf per square mile than anywhere in Africa. Pairs naturally with Kruger for a bush-and-beach fortnight; the national park is small but worth a morning.
Lemurs, baobabs and limestone tsingy, with a round in the hills above the capital.

Nothing here lives anywhere else: the indri calling through the rainforest at Andasibe, ring-tailed lemurs on the granite at Anja, the stone forest of Bemaraha. One mature course sits twenty kilometres from Antananarivo, and the islands off Nosy Be finish the trip on the beach. Pairs with Mauritius in a single flight.

Marrakech alone has three courses we would cross a continent for, with the snow of the High Atlas behind every green. From there the desert begins: the stone plateau of the Agafay half an hour from the city, the Draa Valley and its kasbahs, and the great dunes of Erg Chebbi and Erg Chigaga for a night under the Sahara's stars. Add Rabat, Mazagan or the Atlantic cliffs at Taghazout for more golf.
West Africa's best savanna safari, a lagoon village on stilts, and a brand-new championship course.

Benin is the surprise on the list. Pendjari, run by African Parks, is the strongest big-game safari in West Africa, with elephant, lion, buffalo and hippo in the dry season. Cotonou has the pirogue city of Ganvié on the lagoon and the slave-route history of Ouidah, and the country's first eighteen-hole course now runs between the lagoon and the Atlantic at Avlékété.
Rebuilt from the old Nyarutarama course into the best-conditioned layout in East Africa, ten minutes from the city centre.
Gaborone's championship course, for guests routing through the capital before the Delta.
Ten minutes from the Zambian side of the Falls, with zebra and impala on the fairways and a colonial clubhouse.
Host of the Zambia Open, a mature parkland course on the way to the Lower Zambezi.
The capital's championship course, on the edge of the Khomas highlands, and the opening round before Sossusvlei.
One of only a handful of true desert courses in the world, green fairways cut into the Namib dunes beside the Swakop River.
The oldest course in the south, laid out under the Pasha of Marrakech between cypress, olive and orange trees, with the Atlas on the skyline. Churchill and Eisenhower both played here.
Desert-style golf in the foothills above the Agafay, fifteen minutes from the medina and regularly ranked the best course in Morocco. Firm, fast and framed by snow peaks.
Ten minutes from the city, with contemporary sculpture set among the water features and the clubhouse of a Moroccan riad. The easy round on arrival day.
The Red Course in Rabat's cork-oak forest is the home of the Hassan II Trophy and the country's championship test: long, tree-lined and immaculately kept.
Links-style golf on the Atlantic dunes at El Jadida, an hour south of Casablanca, with the ocean on one side and the resort's beach on the other.
Clifftop holes above the surf north of Agadir, with argan trees between the fairways and the Atlantic beneath the greens. The best coastal round in the country.
At 1,650 metres among the cedar forests of Ifrane in the Middle Atlas, with Barbary macaques in the trees and snow on the greens in January.
The country's only eighteen, on the rolling hills of Andakana twenty kilometres from Antananarivo. Undulating, natural, with a small hotel at the clubhouse for the night before the forest.

Benin's first eighteen-hole course, routed between the lagoon and the Atlantic west of Cotonou around protected trees and a sacred grove. Long and open; we confirm tee times at booking while it settles in.
The river crossings, and the private conservancies where the cats are the point.
Africa's most famous reserve. The private conservancies north of the river allow off-road tracking and night drives with a fraction of the vehicles.
The classic postcard of Africa: elephant herds crossing the plains with the mountain behind. Small, reliable and close to Nairobi.
Walk with the rangers who protect the rhino.
The conservancies of the Laikipia plateau hold the densest rhino populations in East Africa, with walking, horse-riding and night drives allowed.
1 hour from Great Rift Valley Lodge
Flamingos on the soda lake, rhino in the acacia forest.
A compact Rift Valley park that pairs neatly with a round at Great Rift Valley Lodge on the drive from Nairobi.
The dry-country species you see nowhere else.
Semi-arid northern Kenya along the Ewaso Nyiro river, with the 'Samburu special five' and some of the best leopard viewing in the country.
Red-dust elephants on the way to the coast.
Kenya's largest park, on the road and rail line between Nairobi and Mombasa. The natural bridge between a Nairobi golf week and Vipingo Ridge.
The greatest wildlife stage on earth.
Endless plains, two million animals on the move, and the highest density of big cats in Africa. Allow four nights and move camps with the herds.
A day on the crater floor.
A collapsed volcano holding the densest concentration of large mammals in Africa. Stay on the rim and descend at dawn before the day visitors.
Underrated and close to Arusha, with some of the largest elephant herds in the north and a river that draws everything in the dry season.
Tree-climbing lions and a lakeshore of birds.
A small, pretty park between Tarangire and the Crater, ideal for a half-day on the road to Ngorongoro.
Tanzania's wild south, with ten per cent of Africa's lions.
Vast, remote and almost empty of other vehicles. For second-time safari-goers who want the bush to themselves.
Safari by boat on the Rufiji.
The largest protected area in Africa, with boat, walking and fly-camping safaris. The natural pairing with Zanzibar's golf and beach.
An hour with a gorilla family.
Half the world's remaining mountain gorillas live in this ancient forest. Permits are limited and we hold an allocation for our guests.
Savanna, crater lakes and the channel between two lakes with the highest concentration of hippo in Africa. Two hours from Bwindi.
The Nile forced through a seven-metre gap.
Uganda's largest park, where the Nile explodes through a gorge. Boat safaris to the foot of the falls and open savanna north of the river.
The primate capital of East Africa. A morning with a habituated chimp community pairs with Queen Elizabeth next door.
Gorillas on the slopes of the Virungas.
Where Dian Fossey worked. The treks are shorter and gentler than Bwindi's, the lodges are the finest in the region, and Kigali's course is on the way.
Lakes, wetlands and savanna on the Tanzanian border, restocked with lion and rhino. A classic safari to balance the gorillas.
The canopy walk above an ancient rainforest.
One of Africa's oldest forests, with chimpanzees, thirteen primate species and a tea-country drive to get there.
Skukuza Golf is inside the park
The Big Five, and nine holes inside the park.
The size of Wales and the most accessible great park in Africa. Skukuza's unfenced course is a round like no other.
Private reserve on Kruger's western boundary where leopard viewing was pioneered. Off-road tracking, night drives and the finest lodges in the country.
The white lions of the Timbavati.
Quieter than the Sabi Sand, sharing an unfenced border with Kruger and famous for its rare white lions.
Malaria-free Big Five, a short hop from Johannesburg.
Malaria-free and family-friendly on the Botswana border, with one of the strongest wild dog populations in the country.
Six hundred elephants at the end of the Garden Route.
Malaria-free and an easy drive from Fancourt, with a marine section that adds whales and great white sharks to the list.
Cheetah in the sand forest, the ocean an hour away.
Seven habitats in one reserve on the KwaZulu-Natal coast, with the best cheetah viewing in the country and scuba diving at Sodwana.
Feb – Jun (full flow), Aug – Oct (clear views)
The smoke that thunders, next to the first tee.
The rainforest path along the lip of the Falls, a sunset cruise above them, and Elephant Hills Golf five minutes up the road.
Forty thousand elephants and almost no one else.
Zimbabwe's largest park, with huge elephant herds at the pumped waterholes in the dry season and some of the best guides in Africa.
Light aircraft from Harare or Victoria Falls
Walking and canoeing on the Zambezi floodplain.
A World Heritage Site where you walk among elephants beneath the albida trees and canoe past hippo on the Zambezi.
Africa's largest elephant population, from the water.
The riverfront is the show: every afternoon by electric boat as the herds come down to drink, the 4x4 for dawn.
A river that ends in the desert.
The world's largest inland delta, explored by mokoro, boat and 4x4 from private concessions reached only by air. The pinnacle of exclusivity.
Quad bikes on the salt pans, meerkats at dawn.
An ancient lake bed the size of Portugal. Sleep out under the stars on the pans and sit with habituated meerkats in the morning.
Black-maned lions in the green season.
One of the largest reserves in the world, at its best after the rains when the pans fill and the predators follow the springbok.
The home of the walking safari.
Where walking safaris were invented, with the highest leopard density in Africa and night drives still permitted. Bush camps on the river bend.
Canoeing past elephants on the Zambezi.
Opposite Mana Pools, with canoe safaris, tiger fishing and elephants wading between the islands.
The Falls from the Zambian side, and Livingstone's rhino.
The small park that holds the Zambian side of the Falls and the country's only white rhino, walkable with a ranger.
Waterholes on the edge of a salt pan.
A vast white pan ringed by waterholes where everything comes to drink. The floodlit waterholes at the camps are a safari in themselves after dark.
The tallest dunes on earth at sunrise.
Not a wildlife safari but the landscape of a lifetime: red dunes, the dead trees of Deadvlei, and the darkest skies in Africa.
Community conservancies in the rocky north-west, with desert elephants in the dry riverbeds and the most successful rhino conservation story in Africa.
The island's last rainforest, above the Heritage courses.
Hiking trails, waterfalls and the pink pigeon and Mauritius kestrel, both brought back from near-extinction. A morning away from the course.
The indri's dawn song through the rainforest.
The largest living lemur sings at first light, and the forest is small enough that you will hear it from your lodge. Night walks find chameleons and mouse lemurs on the forest edge.
A day south on the RN7, or via Fianarantsoa
Ring-tailed lemurs on the granite at close range.
A village-run reserve where habituated troops of ring-tailed lemurs sun themselves on the rocks at eye level. A two-hour walk that pays for the community's school.
Montane rainforest and the rarest lemurs.
Steep, misty and full of life: twelve lemur species including the golden bamboo lemur that led to the park's creation, and chameleons on every night walk.
Flight to Toliara then 4 hours, or 2 days by road
Canyons, natural pools and the sunset window.
Eroded sandstone massif in the south, with walks to swimming pools in the canyons, sifaka in the palms, and the rock window where everyone gathers for sunset.
Kirindy Forest & Avenue of the Baobabs
The baobab avenue at dusk, fossa in the dry forest.
The country's most photographed road, and twenty minutes on, the dry forest where Madagascar's top predator, the fossa, is seen more reliably than anywhere else.
Charter, or Morondava then a day by 4x4
Rope bridges over a forest of stone needles.
A World Heritage limestone labyrinth climbed on fixed cables and suspension bridges. Remote and dry-season only, which is why it is worth the effort.
Black lemurs in the morning, whale sharks after lunch.
The island archipelago off the north-west: a lemur reserve reached by pirogue, reefs, humpbacks in winter and whale sharks in the last months of the year, with private-island lodges to finish.
Desert at the end of the day's round.
A rock-and-dust plateau half an hour from the city that turns gold at sunset, with luxury tented camps for dinner and a night under the stars. The easiest desert in Africa to add to a golf day.
Flight Marrakech–Errachidia then 2 hours, or 2 days via the Dadès gorges
A night in a tented camp among 150-metre dunes.
The classic Sahara: a sea of orange dunes on the Algerian border, reached by camel at sunset, with a luxury camp among them and sand-boarding and 4x4 at dawn.
8 hours via the Draa Valley, or charter to Zagora
The wild erg: no road, no village, forty kilometres of sand.
The bigger, emptier dune field at the end of the Draa Valley. The drive down past the kasbahs and palm groves is the safari; the camp is the reward.
North Africa's highest peaks, ninety minutes from the first tee.
Walking from Imlil through walnut terraces and Berber villages below the 4,167-metre summit. A day walk or a two-night kasbah stay between rounds.
Barbary macaques in the Atlas cedars.
The Middle Atlas cedar forest, with its endemic macaques, crater lakes and the alpine town of Ifrane. Cool, green and a world away from the desert.
The last wild colony of the northern bald ibis.
Estuary, cliffs and dunes south of Agadir, with reintroduced Saharan antelope and the world's most important colony of one of its rarest birds.
Flight Cotonou–Natitingou then 1 hour, or a long day by road
West Africa's best savanna safari, run by African Parks.

Part of the W-Arly-Pendjari complex, the largest intact savanna in West Africa. Wildlife has rebounded since African Parks took over management; game drives in the dry season find elephant, lion and large herds of buffalo. We check the latest travel advice before every departure.
The far north: savanna, river and no other vehicles.

Named for the double bend of the Niger, shared with Niger and Burkina Faso. Remote and lightly visited, with the Mekrou river and its hippos as the centrepiece. Combined with Pendjari for a week in the north.
A city of 30,000 people built on the water.

Ganvié's stilt houses, markets and schools are reached by pirogue across the lagoon, with herons and kingfishers on the fish traps. A morning from the course, and one of the great sights of West Africa.
Safari first, golf woven through. Golf and safari journeys across thirteen African countries, built one guest at a time by people who have played and slept their way across all of it.
